rationale: The IUPHAR classification relates hallucinations to serotonin receptor pharmacology across ligands and clinical contexts. It does not compare dried fig ingestion or measure repeated visual episodes in Parkinson disease.

The review compares imaging patterns across sporadic and familial parkinsonisms. Visual hallucinations help characterize Lewy body syndromes in this discussion. The reviewed diagnostic patterns provide no food exposure comparison.

The review examines retinal structure and imaging markers across neurodegenerative diseases. Clinical visual phenomena and retinal abnormalities represent different observations from counted visual hallucinations after food ingestion.

The study compares structural brain connectivity in dementia with Lewy bodies and comparator groups. Its network outcomes describe disease-related differences. There is no timed dried fig intake or visual episode response.

The review evaluates cerebrospinal fluid and plasma amyloid beta 42 for specialist-service differentiation of Alzheimer dementia and other dementia syndromes. The comparisons are diagnostic biomarker contrasts. They supply no post-ingestion visual outcome.

The article considers round-the-clock levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel and summarizes management experience. Hallucinations may worsen during this drug regimen in some patients. The drug and its delivery route are recorded as pharmacologic context.

Nine Chinese memory clinics contributed 8,405 records, including 455 patients with Lewy body dementia. The report compares clinical characteristics, cognition and imaging findings across diagnoses. The analysis does not establish a temporal culinary exposure.

Neuropsychiatric and cognitive findings were recorded in 328 Parkinson participants at baseline. Of 202 participants without dementia followed for up to four years, 51 developed dementia. Participant, caregiver and clinician instruments supplied different observations. The strongest neuropsychiatric predictor was the total NPI score, with AUC 0.66 (95% CI 0.57–0.75). Hallucination questionnaire scores added little predictive information for dementia. These analyses do not count visual episodes against food intake.

The study examined 112 participants with cognitive impairment and subjective hearing loss, comparing hearing classification with cognitive tests, MRI and amyloid PET. The sensory phenotype is auditory. No edible fig contrast or timed visual hallucination outcome appears.
The existing catalog record describes clinical history and neuroimaging observations in Parkinson cognition. The review does not test dried figs or food-timed visual episodes.

The report reviews stimulation and other procedures in older adults with Parkinson disease. Hallucination risk informs selection and care. The interventions are procedures, with no dried fig exposure.

The author discusses whether AI can outperform clinical neurology and the difficulty of observing a patient's experience of hallucinations. The perspective contains no food experiment, symptom-frequency cohort or other exposure contrast.

The case records dream enactment in pallido-nigro-luysian degeneration and tau proteinopathy. Sleep behavior and neuropathology do not measure waking visual hallucination frequency following a food exposure.

The imaging sample comprised 36 probable dementia-with-Lewy-bodies cases, 15 probable mild cognitive impairment with Lewy-body features, 11 idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder cases and 102 controls. Diagnostic features and MRI susceptibility measurements provide phenotype context. The study does not measure the frozen food or outcome contrast.

The review traces studies of nucleus basalis of Meynert stimulation, including an earlier randomized six-person Parkinson dementia study. Two participants in that report experienced immediate visual symptom improvement. This is a secondary report of the same participants and an electrical stimulation exposure.

The investigators used injected fluorescent ARCAM-1 to assist visualization of amyloid-containing retinal deposits in APP/PS1 mice and controls. The imaging signal measures deposits. It supplies no observation of culinary fig intake or human visual hallucinations.

One hundred participants across ALS, ALS–FTD, behavioral-variant FTD and control groups supplied clinical psychosis and network phenotypes. The original population, sensory comparisons and absence of a timed culinary exposure limit transfer to this claim.

The study considered 190 probable dementia-with-Lewy-bodies cases and 2,552 controls. Genetic risk and Alzheimer co-pathology were compared with clinical features. Hallucination strata describe phenotype, without a dried food intervention or an episode-frequency response.

The report characterizes Perry disease, a DCTN1-associated disorder, from clinical, pathologic and genetic observations. Clinical features and their distribution are relevant to differential diagnosis. The report contains no timed culinary fig contrast.

The trials examine delivery of mental health support by primary-level workers in low- and middle-income countries. Intervention delivery and psychiatric outcomes are distinct from an edible fig exposure or a Parkinson visual episode measure.

The analyzed task sample included 31 participants with Lewy body dementia (13 Parkinson dementia and 18 dementia with Lewy bodies), 16 with Alzheimer disease and 23 controls. The article reports reuse of a previously described cohort. Visual attention task performance and modeled sensory evidence accumulation do not measure visual episode counts after fig ingestion.

Investigators identified prior bipolar disorder in 250 of 2,660 Parkinson patients and compared phenotype by history. The groups differ in psychiatric and medication context, including psychotic symptoms. The study does not isolate dried food intake or repeated visual episodes after ingestion.

The study compares 10 dementia-with-Lewy-bodies participants reporting a sensed presence and 24 without it. It describes sensed presence as perceiving somebody nearby without seeing or hearing them. The PET and clinical comparisons are context for separating this experience from visual episodes.

Visual hallucinations emerged during a clinical course of rapidly progressive parkinsonism with the PRNP D178N variant, with medication changes also reported. The case serves as differential-diagnosis context. It supplies no dried fig exposure comparison.

The review describes cholinergic anatomy, imaging and symptom patterns in Parkinson disease. Prior clinical hallucination findings are collected as neurologic context. The report supplies no dated, exposure-linked dried fig comparison.

The review describes psychiatric symptoms and treatment across disorders and the COVID-19 period. General discussions of psychosis or treatment adverse events do not measure the frozen Parkinson symptom following fig ingestion.

In the Parkinson case, the authors report that daytime visual hallucinations and dream enactment ceased two days after oral TJ-26 Keishikaryukotsuboreito began. The six-month statement reports continued use, stable concurrent Parkinson medicines and no parasomnia recurrence. It supplies no separate six-month visual episode count. Table 2 lists cinnamon bark, peony root, jujube, oyster shell, longgu, licorice root and ginger. The granules contained no fig, with no magnesium composition reported. One uncontrolled case cannot attribute the observation to an individual constituent.

The study uses PET and SPECT with 3D convolutional neural networks to classify diagnostic groups including Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. Classifier performance concerns disease categories. It supplies no clinical food comparison or post-exposure visual episodes.

The study compares visuospatial performance and dopamine-transporter imaging in early Parkinson disease. Task performance and regional transporter measures provide context for visual function. They do not record counted hallucinations following fig ingestion.

This review organizes eye and visual findings across movement disorders. Pantothenate kinase appears in the name of a neurodegenerative disorder. The discussion contains no dietary B5 or fig intervention and no timed visual hallucinations after ingestion.
The existing catalog record includes a clinical table mentioning ophthalmic hallucinations. Molecular pathway and biomarker summaries do not provide a dried fig ingestion comparison.

The review surveys clinical features, diagnostic questions and therapeutic targets in dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson dementia. Clinical descriptions and investigational drugs provide context, without a fig comparison or food-timed visual episode count.

The study compares functional brain network organization among dementia-with-Lewy-bodies, Alzheimer and control groups. Network and diagnostic outcomes provide phenotype context. No timed dietary exposure or visual episode comparison was studied.

This analysis pools prior Japanese zonisamide trials JapicCTI-122040 and JapicCTI-152839 to evaluate axial motor symptoms in dementia with Lewy bodies and parkinsonism. Visual hallucinations provide clinical background. The pooled motor contrast supplies no dried fig or separately counted visual episode evidence.

Thirty participants with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder underwent perfusion SPECT. The outcomes describe progression to neurodegenerative dementia and prediction from baseline imaging. These outcomes do not measure visual episode frequency in people who consumed figs.

The review discusses imaging in targeting and evaluating deep brain stimulation. The Parkinson dementia hallucination observation traces to an earlier six-person trial cited elsewhere in this intake. The review supplies no new patients or culinary exposure contrast.
